name: Azimut 42
description:
The Azimut 42 is an Italian-built flybridge that suits the Ayia Napa day-charter run almost perfectly. At 12.8 metres she takes 11 guests, with two cabins and two bathrooms below deck so your group has somewhere to change and freshen up, and a crew of two who handle the boat so nobody in the party has to.

A typical day leaves Ayia Napa harbour for the sea caves and the natural rock arch at Cape Greco, anchors over the turquoise shallows of the Blue Lagoon for the long swim stop and lunch on board, then finishes in the sheltered horseshoe of Konnos Bay. An underwater scooter and a paddleboard come with the boat, along with snorkelling masks and towels.

Rates run from €800 for two hours to €2,500 for a full eight-hour day, with fuel for the Ayia Napa–Protaras area already included. An overnight stay is €4,200 and a full week is €22,000. Chilled prosecco, local beer, soft drinks and seasonal fruit are served on board as standard.

name: Princess 61
description:
Twenty-four guests is a lot of people to get comfortably onto one boat, and the Princess 61 is the answer to that problem in Ayia Napa. Nineteen metres of British-built flybridge, three cabins, three bathrooms and a crew of three — enough space and enough hands that a large group never feels like a crowd.

She is the boat to book when the occasion matters: a milestone birthday, a wedding party, a company day out. The layout gives you a proper saloon, shaded cockpit seating and a flybridge for anyone who wants the view and the breeze, so guests can spread out instead of stacking up in one corner.

Half a day out of Ayia Napa covers Cape Greco, the Blue Lagoon and Konnos Bay comfortably. Two hours costs €1,200, a full eight-hour day €4,000, and an overnight €5,800; a week aboard is €30,000. Fuel, an experienced captain, snorkelling gear, an underwater scooter, a paddleboard, prosecco, local beer, soft drinks and seasonal fruit are all included.

name: Sea Ray 37.5
description:
If you want a private boat in Ayia Napa without a superyacht budget, the Sea Ray 37.5 is where the fleet starts. Two hours costs €500 and a full eight-hour day €1,900 — and that is the whole boat, not a seat on a shared cruise.

At 11.2 metres she carries 11 guests with two cabins and a bathroom below, run by a crew of two. The scale is the point: small enough to slip into the coves along Cape Greco that bigger yachts have to admire from a distance, big enough that a family or a group of friends can spend a full day aboard without feeling boxed in.

The inclusions do not get trimmed to match the price. Fuel, an experienced captain, snorkelling masks, towels, an underwater scooter and a stand-up paddleboard all come with the charter, as do sparkling wine, local beer, soft drinks and seasonal fruit. For a first time renting a boat in Cyprus, it is the easiest place to begin.

name: Sea Ray 63
description:
Twenty metres and 22 guests put the Sea Ray 63 among the largest boats working out of Ayia Napa, and the deck space is what you notice first — a wide cockpit, generous sunbathing areas and room for people to move around each other on a busy day.

Two cabins and two bathrooms serve the group, and a crew of three means service continues while the captain concentrates on the boat. That matters on a longer charter, when a party of twenty needs drinks poured and the tender managed as well as a course steered.

The run east from Ayia Napa harbour takes in the Cape Greco caves, the Blue Lagoon and Konnos Bay. Two hours is €1,000, eight hours €3,800, and staying out overnight €5,500. Fuel is covered, along with snorkelling masks, towels, an underwater scooter, a paddleboard, sparkling wine, local beer, soft drinks and seasonal fruit.

name: Sea Ray 45.5
description:
The Sea Ray 45.5 sits at the point where a day charter in Ayia Napa stops being a compromise. Fourteen metres, 16 guests, two cabins and two bathrooms, a crew of two — and an eight-hour day at €1,900, which is less than some boats here charge for four.

She is a practical choice for a mixed group. There is shade when the afternoon gets hot, open deck for anyone chasing the sun, and enough seating that sixteen people are not negotiating for space. The swim platform aft makes getting in and out of the water easy for children and less confident swimmers alike.

Days out follow the classic Ayia Napa route to the Cape Greco caves, the Blue Lagoon and Konnos Bay. Rates begin at €600 for two hours. Fuel, an experienced captain, snorkelling masks, an underwater scooter, a paddleboard, sparkling wine, local beer, soft drinks and seasonal fruit are included; bring your own towels for this one.

name: Azimut 46
description:
Getting to the boat is part of the booking on the Azimut 46 — a transfer is included in the charter, so your group is collected and delivered rather than working out parking at the harbour. For a party of twenty arriving from scattered hotels, that is not a small detail.

She is 14.5 metres of Azimut flybridge based in Ayia Napa, taking up to 20 guests with two cabins, two bathrooms and a crew of two. The flybridge is the draw: an upper deck with its own seating and the best view of the coast as you run out toward Cape Greco.

Two hours costs €800 and a full eight-hour day €2,500, with an overnight at €3,800. Fuel for the Ayia Napa–Protaras area, an experienced captain, snorkelling masks, towels, soft drinks, water and seasonal fruit are all part of the price. A day typically takes in the sea caves at Cape Greco, the Blue Lagoon and a final swim at Konnos Bay.

name: Azimut 62
description:
Fifteen guests on a twenty-metre yacht is a deliberately generous ratio, and it is what makes the Azimut 62 feel different from the rest of the Ayia Napa fleet. Three cabins, two bathrooms and a crew of three serving a relatively small party — this is a boat chartered for comfort rather than capacity.

Charters start at three hours rather than two, which reflects how she is used: unhurried days rather than quick harbour hops. Three hours is €1,900, rising to €4,100 for eight hours, with an overnight at €6,500.

The extra length shows in the ride. She holds her line in the afternoon chop that builds off Cape Greco, so the run out to the Blue Lagoon and back stays comfortable when smaller boats are working. Fuel, an experienced captain, snorkelling masks, towels, a paddleboard, sparkling wine, local beer, soft drinks and seasonal fruit are included.

name: Napa Blue
description:
Napa Blue carries 50 guests — more than double most boats in the Ayia Napa fleet — and that single number explains what she is for. This is the vessel for the party, the corporate day out, the group too large for anything else on this coast.

At 21 metres with a crew of five, she is run more like a venue than a yacht. The deck is laid out for people standing, moving and mixing rather than sitting in a fixed cockpit, and five crew means fifty guests are actually looked after. Two cabins and two bathrooms serve the group.

Pricing reflects the scale: €1,600 for two hours, €5,000 for a full eight-hour day, €7,500 overnight. Fuel, an experienced captain, snorkelling masks, soft drinks and water are included — catering and bar beyond that are usually arranged to suit the event, so tell us what you have in mind. Days run out to Cape Greco, the Blue Lagoon and Konnos Bay.

name: Ferreti 592
description:
The Ferreti 592 is the flagship of the Protaras fleet, and the week-long rate of €38,000 places her accordingly. Eighteen and a half metres of Italian build, three cabins, two bathrooms, 25 guests and a crew of three.

Protaras is the gentler end of this coast. Days begin in the calm, shallow water off Pernera, anchor over the turquoise of Fig Tree Bay for the first swim, take in the clear snorkelling at Green Bay, then round the national-park headland at Cape Greco for lunch in a protected cove before a last stop at Konnos Bay.

She is equipped for a full day rather than a quick outing: an underwater scooter and paddleboard aboard, snorkelling masks and towels for the group, sparkling wine, local beer, soft drinks and seasonal fruit served as standard, and fuel included. Two hours costs €1,400, eight hours €4,700, and an overnight €6,800.

name: Sunseeker 50
description:
Limassol is the island's marina capital, and the Sunseeker 50 is the boat to see it from. Sixteen metres, 12 guests, two cabins, two bathrooms and a crew of two, berthed in the heart of the city.

Charters here have a character of their own. You cast off from Limassol Marina and clear the breakwater into open water, then run west to drift into the sheltered bay below Cape Gata — Akrotiri Bay, where the water settles and lunch on board can stretch out as long as you like. The return is timed for the light, a gentle sunset cruise back into the marina.

Rates are among the most reasonable for a yacht this size: €900 for three hours, €1,800 for a full eight-hour day. Fuel, an experienced captain, snorkelling masks, a stand-up paddleboard, soft drinks and water are included. With 12 guests aboard a 16-metre hull, there is genuine room to spread out.

name: Sea Ray 62
description:
The Sea Ray 62 charters out of Latsi, the small fishing harbour that is the gateway to the Akamas — the wildest and least developed coastline in Cyprus, reachable properly only by boat.

Eighteen metres and just 12 guests makes her one of the roomiest boats per head in the fleet, with two cabins, two bathrooms and a crew of two. Days run along the peninsula to the Blue Lagoon, where the anchor goes down over glowing turquoise for snorkelling, swimming and jumping off the boat, then on to the hidden coves and sea caves of the protected coast for lunch aboard.

Rates start at €1,700 for two hours and reach €4,100 for six; an overnight is €4,500. Fuel, an experienced captain, snorkelling masks, soft drinks, water and seasonal fruit are included. The Akamas is a national park, so this stretch of coast stays quiet in a way the south simply does not.

name: Sunseeker Manhattan 54
description:
Sixteen metres of Sunseeker Manhattan, 16 guests, two cabins, two bathrooms and a crew of two — the Manhattan 54 is the balanced choice for a day on the Akamas coast out of Latsi.

The Manhattan layout is built around the saloon and a large shaded cockpit, which is exactly right for this stretch of water: you are out for hours, the sun is unrelenting by midday, and having proper shade to retreat into changes how the day feels. The bathing platform aft opens straight onto the water at the Blue Lagoon.

A day here runs from Latsi harbour along the wild peninsula to the Blue Lagoon for the main swim, then into the Akamas coves for lunch at anchor. Two hours costs €1,300, eight hours €3,800, an overnight €5,000. Fuel, an experienced captain, snorkelling masks, towels, sparkling wine, local beer, soft drinks and seasonal fruit are all included.

name: Sea Ray 52
description:
A transfer comes with the Sea Ray 52, which is worth more in Latsi than almost anywhere else on the island — the harbour is a long drive from most resorts, and having 20 guests collected rather than convoying up the coast makes the day start properly.

She is 16 metres with two cabins, two bathrooms and a crew of two. Charters are priced for the shape of an Akamas day: €1,500 for two hours, €2,600 for four, and €2,890 for six, with an overnight at €3,200 — a modest step up that turns the trip into a night at anchor.

The route is the reason people come to Latsi. Out along the Akamas peninsula, anchor in the Blue Lagoon for the long swim and snorkel, then the protected coves and sea caves before a scenic run home. An experienced captain, snorkelling masks, towels, soft drinks, water and seasonal fruit are included.

name: Sunseeker 50 Destiny
description:
Destiny is a 16-metre Sunseeker working out of Paphos harbour, and she takes 20 guests — an unusually high number for a boat this size, which keeps the cost per person down for larger groups.

The Paphos coast is the most scenic in Cyprus for a day charter. You slip out beneath the castle and turn north along the archaeological coast, anchoring off the honeycomb of sea caves at Coral Bay for the first swim and snorkel. Longer charters push on to the wild protected sands of Lara Bay, a turtle-nesting reserve, or turn south to drift beneath Aphrodite's Rock at Petra tou Romiou.

Two hours costs €800, four hours €1,600 and six hours €2,400, with two cabins, two bathrooms and a crew of two aboard. Fuel, an experienced captain, snorkelling masks and towels are included. For a group wanting the Paphos coastline without a long day at sea, the four-hour charter covers the caves comfortably.

name: Ocean Dream
description:
Ocean Dream is a twenty-metre yacht based in Paphos with three cabins, two bathrooms and capacity for 22 guests — the largest cabin count in the Paphos fleet, which makes her the practical choice when an overnight is on the table at €5,100.

Three cabins change what a charter can be. A day trip to the Coral Bay caves and Lara Bay becomes a night at anchor and a second morning on the water, with somewhere proper for people to sleep rather than a token berth below.

By day she runs the classic Paphos route: out past the castle, north along the archaeological coast to the sea caves for snorkelling, then the turtle beach at Lara or south to Aphrodite's Rock depending on the wind. Two hours costs €1,500 and six hours €3,100, with a crew of two aboard. Fuel, an experienced captain, snorkelling masks and towels are included.

name: Kurosivo IV
description:
At 22 metres, Kurosivo IV is the longest boat in the fleet, and she is configured entirely for daytime capacity — 35 guests, no cabins, two bathrooms and a crew of two. Every metre goes into deck rather than accommodation.

That trade-off produces the best value on this coast for a large group. Two hours costs €720 and six hours €2,000, which for 35 people works out lower per head than almost anything else available in Paphos. For a family reunion, a club outing or a group of friends who simply want a big open boat for the afternoon, the maths is hard to argue with.

She runs the Paphos coastline north to the Coral Bay sea caves for snorkelling and swimming, with the option of continuing to Lara Bay on the longer charters. Fuel, an experienced captain and snorkelling masks are included; food and drink are usually brought aboard or arranged to suit the group.

name: Latchi Icon
description:
Latchi Icon is the most affordable way onto the Akamas coast: €695 for two hours and €1,295 for six, on a 12.5-metre boat licensed for 16 guests with a single cabin, a bathroom and a skipper.

What makes her stand out is that the inclusions do not thin out to match the price. Sparkling wine, local beer, soft drinks, seasonal fruit, towels and snorkelling masks all come with the charter, and fuel is covered — a list that several boats at twice the rate do not match.

Latsi is the departure point for the Blue Lagoon, and on a boat this size you reach it in comfortable time and anchor close in. The day takes in the lagoon itself, the hidden coves along the protected Akamas shoreline, and the sea caves that punctuate the peninsula, before a scenic run back to the harbour. For couples and small families it is the easiest introduction to chartering a boat in western Cyprus.

name: Rodman 38
description:
The Rodman 38 is a working boat's answer to a day charter — twelve metres, solidly built, taking 15 guests along the Akamas coast from Latsi with a crew of two.

Charters come in three lengths and nothing else: three hours at €1,050, four at €1,300, or six at €1,680. The simplicity is deliberate. The three-hour trip gets you to the Blue Lagoon and back with a proper swim stop; six hours adds the Akamas coves, the sea caves and a long lunch at anchor without rushing any of it.

One cabin and one bathroom serve the group, with an experienced captain, snorkelling masks, towels, seasonal fruit and fuel included. She is a sensible choice for a group that wants time in the water rather than a floating lounge — the Akamas is a national park, and the coastline you cross to reach the lagoon is as much the point as the destination.

name: Ferreti 67
description:
Thirty-five guests, three cabins and three bathrooms make the Ferreti 67 the boat for the largest parties leaving Protaras. At twenty metres with a crew of three, she handles numbers that would overwhelm most of the fleet.

Three bathrooms is the specification that matters here and rarely gets mentioned. On a six-hour charter with thirty-five people aboard, it is the difference between a comfortable day and a permanent queue.

Protaras offers the calmest water on this coast, which suits a large mixed group with children. Days start in the shallows off Pernera, anchor over Fig Tree Bay for the first swim, take in Green Bay for easy snorkelling near the surface, then round to Cape Greco for lunch in a protected cove and a final stop at Konnos Bay. Two hours costs €1,500, six hours €3,100 and an overnight €5,100, with fuel, an experienced captain, snorkelling masks and towels included.

name: ELYSIAN BLUE
description:
Elysian Blue takes 10 guests — the smallest party in the Ayia Napa fleet — across 13 metres with two cabins and two bathrooms. The ratio is the whole proposition: this is a boat chartered for space rather than headcount.

For a couple, a family or two couples travelling together, it means the day belongs to you. There is no negotiating for a spot on the sunbed, no waiting for the swim ladder, no sharing the shade. The crew of two are looking after ten people instead of twenty-five.

She is fully equipped despite the modest size: a paddleboard aboard, snorkelling masks and towels, sparkling wine, local beer, soft drinks and seasonal fruit, with fuel included. Two hours costs €800, a full eight-hour day €2,500, and an overnight €3,500. The route runs out to the Cape Greco caves, the Blue Lagoon and Konnos Bay — the same coastline as the big boats, at a quieter pace.

name: Azimut 46 Protaras
description:
Food is included on this Azimut 46, which makes her unusual in the Protaras fleet — on most charters catering is an extra to arrange, and here a meal aboard is part of the price.

She is 14 metres with two cabins, two bathrooms, room for 16 guests and a crew of two. Beyond the food, the list is generous: an underwater scooter, a stand-up paddleboard, towels, sparkling wine, local beer, soft drinks, seasonal fruit and fuel are all covered.

That combination suits the way Protaras charters actually run. The water here is sheltered and shallow, the stops are close together — Fig Tree Bay, Green Bay, the coves at Cape Greco, Konnos Bay — so days are spent at anchor swimming and eating rather than covering distance. Two hours costs €1,000 and a full eight-hour day €3,200. If you would rather not organise provisions for sixteen people, this is the straightforward option.

name: Sea Ray 45.6
description:
Fourteen guests across fourteen metres gives the Sea Ray 45.6 an easy middle ground in the Ayia Napa fleet — room to spread out without paying twenty-metre money. Two cabins, two bathrooms and a crew of two aboard.

An eight-hour day costs €2,100 and two hours €700, which puts a full day's charter within reach of a family or a group of friends splitting the cost. The pricing steps evenly through the hours, so a five- or six-hour trip is easy to size to the day you actually want.

The kit aboard is the full set: an underwater scooter, a paddleboard, snorkelling masks, towels, sparkling wine, soft drinks, seasonal fruit and fuel included. Charters follow the eastern coastline from Ayia Napa harbour to the sea caves and rock arch at Cape Greco, the Blue Lagoon for the main swim stop, and Konnos Bay for a last dip before heading in.

name: AG Queen
description:
Four cabins on an eleven-metre boat is an unusual specification, and it tells you exactly what AG Queen is for. She is the fleet's overnight and multi-day specialist — 10 guests, four cabins, three bathrooms and a crew of two.

The rates follow the same logic. There is no two-hour option; charters begin at four hours for €1,790 and six for €2,190, but the numbers that matter are €3,600 for an overnight and €13,900 for a full week. That weekly rate is the lowest in the fleet by a wide margin, which makes her the practical choice for a genuine sailing holiday rather than an afternoon out.

Based in Ayia Napa, she gives you the Cape Greco caves, the Blue Lagoon and Konnos Bay on the first day and the freedom to keep going after that. Fuel, an experienced captain, snorkelling masks, towels, a paddleboard, sparkling wine, soft drinks and seasonal fruit are included.

name: Galeon 375 GTO
description:
The Galeon 375 GTO is the most modern-feeling boat in the Ayia Napa fleet — a 13-metre Polish-built sports yacht designed around opening up to the water rather than sealing you off from it.

She takes 12 guests with two cabins, two bathrooms and a crew of two. The GTO layout puts the emphasis on the aft deck and the bathing platform, which is where a Cyprus charter is actually spent: swimming at the Blue Lagoon, snorkelling at the Cape Greco caves, and sitting with your feet in the water at anchor in Konnos Bay.

Two hours costs €700 and a full eight-hour day €2,200 — competitive for a boat of this generation. Fuel, an experienced captain, snorkelling masks, towels, an underwater scooter, sparkling wine, local beer, soft drinks and seasonal fruit are all included. For a smaller group that cares how the boat looks and rides, she is the pick of the mid-size charters here.

name: Sea Ray 32
description:
At 10.5 metres the Sea Ray 32 is the smallest boat in the fleet, and for a lot of charters that is the right answer. Eleven guests, two cabins, one bathroom, a crew of two, and a price that starts at €600 for two hours.

Small boats reach places big ones cannot. The coastline between Ayia Napa and Cape Greco is broken by caves, arches and narrow inlets, and a 10.5-metre hull can nose into them properly instead of anchoring offshore and swimming the rest. On a calm morning that access is worth more than another five metres of deck.

A full eight-hour day is €2,100, with the hours priced evenly in between. Fuel, an experienced captain, snorkelling masks, towels, an underwater scooter, sparkling wine, local beer, soft drinks and seasonal fruit are included — the same list as boats three times the price. A good first charter, and a good one for families with young children.

name: Azimut 55
description:
The Azimut 55 is Larnaca's premium charter: 16 metres, three cabins, three bathrooms, 20 guests and a crew of two, priced from €3,000 for four hours.

Larnaca charters have a character the rest of the island cannot offer. You board on the palm-lined seafront and head into a wide, sheltered bay, and the first stop is the Zenobia — the famous wreck lying just off the coast, where you anchor over the hull and snorkel the shallows above it while the crew tells the story. From there the route follows the salt-lake coast south to the quiet bays around Cape Kiti.

Six hours costs €3,500 and an overnight €3,900, which is a small step up for a night at anchor in the bay. Three cabins and three bathrooms make that overnight genuinely comfortable for a group. An experienced captain, snorkelling masks, towels, soft drinks, water and seasonal fruit are included.

name: Calypso
description:
Calypso is the most affordable charter in the fleet — €400 for two hours, €1,600 for a full eight-hour day, for a 14-metre boat licensed to carry 20 guests.

She is built for daytime use: open deck, one bathroom, no cabins, a crew of two. Nothing is given over to accommodation, which is why twenty people fit comfortably on a hull this length and why the price sits where it does. For a group that wants a boat for the day rather than a floating hotel, none of that is a compromise.

Larnaca is the calmest of the charter bases, with a wide sheltered bay and gentle water that suits families and nervous swimmers. Days take in the Zenobia wreck, where you can snorkel above the hull, and the quiet bays down toward Cape Kiti. An experienced captain, snorkelling masks and fuel are included; food and drink are brought aboard, which keeps the total cost down further.

name: Sea Ray SLX 400
description:
The Sea Ray SLX 400 is a bowrider rather than a cabin cruiser, and that changes the day. Thirteen metres of open deck, seating that wraps around the bow, one cabin and one bathroom below for changing — everything arranged around being outside.

For sixteen guests on the Ayia Napa coast, that layout earns its keep. You spend a Cyprus charter in and out of the water, not sheltering indoors, and the SLX gives you sunbathing space forward, a proper swim platform aft, and sightlines all round as you run out to the Cape Greco caves.

Charters start at three hours for €850 and reach €2,050 for a full eight-hour day. Fuel, an experienced captain, snorkelling masks, towels, an underwater scooter, sparkling wine, local beer, soft drinks and seasonal fruit are included. She is a strong choice for a younger group or anyone who would rather be on deck than in a saloon.
